Many people with hay fever could be overlooking a consequence of the higher pollen count,(Image: Getty Images)

The Irish weather service warned of a "pollen bomb" set to grip the nation in the coming days as an expert shared how an increased count can affect sleep.

Many people with hay fever could be overlooking a consequence of the higher pollen count, brought about by a sweltering heatwave gripping Ireland, with temperatures set to soar as high as 30 degrees Celsius (86 degrees Fahrenheit) on Thursday.

Based on Ireland’s population, roughly 800,000 adults are expected to be living with undiagnosed sleep disorders, and insomnia disorder is considered one of the most common mental health conditions in Ireland, affecting approximately 15% of adults. Nervous system expert Dr. Elisabetta Burchi, head of research at neurotechnology company Nurosym, warned about the impact this might have on Ireland’s sleep and recovery.

“Hay fever extends beyond physical discomfort and actually affects the nervous system due to poor sleep and the heightened stress that follows, creating a sleep-stress cycle," she said. "Nasal congestion and heightened inflammation markers cause frequent nighttime awakenings and leave many tossing and turning.”

Keep pollen out of the bedroom — Keep windows closed during peak pollen hours, shower before bed and avoid drying clothes outdoors, as pollen can easily transfer onto bedding and clothing.

• Clear nasal passages before sleep — Saline nasal rinses or sprays can help reduce congestion and make breathing easier overnight.

• Create a cool sleeping environment — Warm temperatures can worsen sleep disruption. Aim to keep bedrooms cool and well-ventilated while limiting pollen exposure.

• Manage stress before bed — Gentle breathing exercises, mindfulness practices or other relaxation techniques may help calm an overactive stress response and make it easier to fall asleep.

• Prioritize recovery after poor sleep — If hay fever has disrupted sleep, avoid relying on excessive caffeine and instead focus on hydration, light physical activity and consistent sleep routines to support recovery.

“When hay fever symptoms repeatedly disrupt sleep, the body’s stress response system becomes inappropriately activated, which can affect mood, cognitive performance, and emotional regulation, particularly in individuals already experiencing high baseline stress,” Dr. Burchi said.

“Throughout the allergy season, many people can become caught in a cycle where allergic inflammation disrupts sleep, poor sleep increases stress sensitivity, and heightened stress amplifies the burden of symptoms," she added. "This ongoing interaction can leave individuals feeling more fatigued, less resilient, and less able to function at their best during the day.”
